Getting started with silverback

Source: vignettes/silverback.Rmd
silverback.Rmd

silverback turns the files you download from the Gorilla Experiment Builder into three tidy tibbles: one for task responses, one for questionnaire answers and one for participants. A typical session looks like this:

library(silverback)

g <- read_gorilla("data_exp_123456-v3.zip")
gorilla_checks(g)
trials <- gorilla_trials(g)
answers <- gorilla_wide(g)
people <- gorilla_participants(g)
write_gorilla(g, "tidy")

The rest of this page goes through each step with a small invented experiment that comes with the package.

library(silverback)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

Download the data from Gorilla

On the Data tab of your experiment, generate the data for the versions you need and download it. Gorilla offers two layouts, one file per node of the experiment tree or combined files with all tasks in one file and all questionnaires in another. Either works as long as you choose CSV. Questionnaires can be downloaded in long or short format.

Unzip the download or leave it as it is. read_gorilla() accepts the ZIP file, the folder or single CSV files. Keep one layout per folder: with both, the same rows would be read twice, and read_gorilla() warns about it.

Read the files

The example experiment has a lexical decision task made with Task Builder 2, a rhyme judgement task made with Task Builder 1, a consent form made with Questionnaire Builder 1 and a background questionnaire made with Questionnaire Builder 2. One branch of the experiment was never reached, so one of the files is empty.

g <- read_gorilla(gorilla_example())
#> Skipped 1 file without data (nodes no participant reached): data_exp_123456-v3_questionnaire-zz1e.csv
g
#> <gorilla_data> experiment 123456, version 3
#> 6 participants
#>   complete: 5, live: 1
#> Tasks:
#>   Lexical decision (Task Builder 2): 6 participants
#>   Rhyme judgement (Task Builder 1): 5 participants
#> Questionnaires:
#>   Background: 7 items, 6 participants
#>   Consent: 2 items, 6 participants
#> 1 empty file skipped

The printout lists the tasks and questionnaires that were found and how many participants did each. Empty files are skipped with a message.

read_gorilla() returns a list of four tables. g$files has one row per file and says which builder each file comes from. g$tasks keeps every row of every task file, g$questionnaires holds one row per questionnaire answer and g$participants one row per participant. You will rarely need the first two directly.

g$files
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   file                        experiment version node  kind  builder task   rows
#>   <chr>                       <chr>      <chr>   <chr> <chr> <chr>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 data_exp_123456-v3_questio… 123456     3       ques… ques… questi… Back…    66
#> 2 data_exp_123456-v3_questio… 123456     3       ques… ques… questi… Cons…    36
#> 3 data_exp_123456-v3_questio… 123456     3       ques… ques… questi… NA        0
#> 4 data_exp_123456-v3_task-ld… 123456     3       task… task  task_b… Lexi…   104
#> 5 data_exp_123456-v3_task-rh… 123456     3       task… task  task_b… Rhym…    90

Column names are converted to snake case, so Participant Private ID becomes participant_private_id. Columns that come from your spreadsheets start with spreadsheet_, and values saved to the store start with store_. Task Builder 1 exports give spreadsheet columns no prefix at all, and silverback adds it so that both builders look the same.

Check the data

Before the analysis it is worth looking at what came in. summary() gives one line per task and questionnaire:

summary(g)
#> 6 participants (complete: 5, live: 1)
#> 
#> Tasks
#>         task_name        builder participants responses_min responses_median
#>  Lexical decision Task Builder 2            6             7               16
#>   Rhyme judgement Task Builder 1            5             8                8
#>  responses_max correct rt_median fast slow minutes
#>             16   0.943     673.1    0    0     0.4
#>              8   0.950     910.1    0    0     0.4
#> 
#> Questionnaires
#>   task_name participants items unanswered
#>  Background            6     7          0
#>     Consent            6     2          0

For tasks, the line shows how many responses each participant gave, the share Gorilla marked as correct, the median reaction time and how long people spent on the task. That share only means something if scoring was set up in Gorilla. For questionnaires, it shows how many items were left unanswered.

gorilla_checks() goes further and lists findings about single participants:

gorilla_checks(g)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   check        participant_private_id task_name       detail                    
#>   <chr>        <chr>                  <chr>           <chr>                     
#> 1 status       9100222                NA              status is live            
#> 2 missing_task 9100222                Rhyme judgement not done, although 2 of 3…

In the example one participant stopped during the lexical decision task. The checks report the status and the missing rhyme judgement task. On real data they also find people who took part twice under the same public ID, who pressed the same key almost every time, who often answered faster than 200 ms, or who used a different type of device from most participants. Randomiser groups of very different sizes are reported too. You can change the thresholds with the function’s arguments. Nothing is removed, so you decide what to exclude.

Get one row per response

Task files hold far more rows than responses. Instructions, fixation crosses, continue buttons and audio events all get rows of their own. gorilla_trials() keeps only the rows with a response:

ld <- gorilla_trials(g, task = "Lexical decision")
ld
#> # A tibble: 87 × 19
#>   participant_private_id experiment_version tree_node_key repeat_key task_name  
#>   <chr>                               <int> <chr>         <chr>      <chr>      
#> 1 9100037                                 3 task-ld2k     NA         Lexical de…
#> 2 9100037                                 3 task-ld2k     NA         Lexical de…
#> 3 9100037                                 3 task-ld2k     NA         Lexical de…
#> 4 9100037                                 3 task-ld2k     NA         Lexical de…
#> 5 9100037                                 3 task-ld2k     NA         Lexical de…
#> 6 9100037                                 3 task-ld2k     NA         Lexical de…
#> # ℹ 81 more rows
#> # ℹ 14 more variables: task_version <int>, spreadsheet <chr>, trial <dbl>,
#> #   display <chr>, screen <chr>, component <chr>, object <chr>, response <chr>,
#> #   rt <dbl>, correct <lgl>, time <dttm>, spreadsheet_word <chr>,
#> #   spreadsheet_lexicality <chr>, spreadsheet_answer <chr>

The first columns are the same for every task, whichever builder it was made with. The table below lists them.

Column Content
participant_private_id Gorilla’s ID for the participant
experiment_version, tree_node_key, repeat_key where in the experiment the response was given
task_name, task_version the task and its version
spreadsheet, trial the spreadsheet and trial number
display, screen the display and screen (Task Builder 1 has no displays)
component, object what recorded the response (zone type and zone name in Task Builder 1)
response, rt, correct the response, the reaction time in ms and whether it was correct
time when the response was given, in UTC

Next come the timing columns that Gorilla recorded for the responses, such as onset_time and response_duration in Task Builder 2 or reaction_onset in Task Builder 1. Columns without values are left out. The invented example has no timing data, so these columns are missing below. The spreadsheet and store columns of the task follow, so the conditions are ready to use:

ld |>
  filter(correct) |>
  summarise(rt = median(rt), .by = spreadsheet_lexicality)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   spreadsheet_lexicality    rt
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>
#> 1 nonword                 723.
#> 2 word                    650.

Leave out task to get the responses of all tasks in one table. If you need the rows around each response, such as the moment an audio file started, use all_rows = TRUE. Every column of the export, including the metadata left out here, remains in g$tasks.

Get one row per participant for questionnaires

gorilla_wide() puts each questionnaire item in its own column:

answers <- gorilla_wide(g)
answers
#> # A tibble: 6 × 14
#>   participant_private_id   age gender gender_quantised languages_english
#>   <chr>                  <int> <chr>             <dbl>             <int>
#> 1 9100037                   23 Female                1                 1
#> 2 9100074                   34 Female                1                 1
#> 3 9100111                   22 Female                1                 1
#> 4 9100148                   26 Male                  2                 1
#> 5 9100185                   29 Female                1                 0
#> 6 9100222                   34 Male                  2                 0
#> # ℹ 9 more variables: languages_german <int>, languages_italian <int>,
#> #   languages_portuguese <int>, handedness <chr>, handedness_quantised <dbl>,
#> #   consent_data <chr>, consent_data_quantised <dbl>, consent_withdraw <chr>,
#> #   consent_withdraw_quantised <dbl>

Dropdowns, multiple choice questions and Likert scales also have a quantised value, the position of the chosen option, which goes into a second column ending in _quantised. Checkboxes give one column per option, such as languages_german. Questionnaires from both builders and in both download formats end up with the same column names.

Sometimes a participant answers an item twice. This happens after a repeated node, or when two questions in the same questionnaire share an object name. The first answer stays in the item’s column and later answers go into columns ending in __2, __3 and so on.

Get one row per participant for everything else

gorilla_participants() collects what Gorilla records about each person:

people <- gorilla_participants(g)
people
#> # A tibble: 6 × 18
#>   participant_private_id participant_public_id    experiment_id
#>   <chr>                  <chr>                            <int>
#> 1 9100037                c805ceab3f4eb9172ecd0b95        123456
#> 2 9100074                1d1c4b74f2b229c3711cbcc8        123456
#> 3 9100111                b48c18f6af1d44ac3fe078e2        123456
#> 4 9100148                cce8638538eef07b5c3ce7a5        123456
#> 5 9100185                7f50b2600354023e074434c0        123456
#> 6 9100222                9b2d42c0a5c131039b4134ea        123456
#> # ℹ 15 more variables: participant_device_type <chr>, participant_device <chr>,
#> #   participant_os <chr>, participant_browser <chr>,
#> #   participant_monitor_size <chr>, participant_viewport_size <chr>,
#> #   local_timezone <int>, experiment_version <int>, participant_status <chr>,
#> #   start <dttm>, end <dttm>, tasks <int>, randomiser_ab12 <chr>,
#> #   store_score <int>, minutes <dbl>

Each row has the participant’s status, device, operating system and browser. It also has the times of the first and last event with the minutes in between, the group that each randomiser or branch node assigned, and the last value of each store field. Columns that are empty for everybody are dropped. status = "complete" keeps only participants who finished.

Put the tables together

The three tables share participant_private_id, so they can be joined with left_join(). Here the background questionnaire and the randomiser group are added to each response:

ld |>
  left_join(select(answers, participant_private_id, age, gender), by = "participant_private_id") |>
  left_join(select(people, participant_private_id, randomiser_ab12), by = "participant_private_id") |>
  select(participant_private_id, spreadsheet_word, rt, age, gender, randomiser_ab12)
#> # A tibble: 87 × 6
#>   participant_private_id spreadsheet_word    rt   age gender randomiser_ab12
#>   <chr>                  <chr>            <dbl> <int> <chr>  <chr>          
#> 1 9100037                mukket            628.    23 Female List A         
#> 2 9100037                venisk            733.    23 Female List A         
#> 3 9100037                mirror            840.    23 Female List A         
#> 4 9100037                drosk            1110.    23 Female List A         
#> 5 9100037                basket            470.    23 Female List A         
#> 6 9100037                pencil            650.    23 Female List A         
#> # ℹ 81 more rows

All three can go straight into dplyr or ggplot2.

Before sharing the data

If you recruited through a platform such as Prolific, the public IDs are the platform’s IDs and can identify people. blind_ids() replaces them, the external session IDs and the completion codes with codes such as P001, consistently across all tables:

blind_ids(g) |>
  gorilla_participants() |>
  select(participant_private_id, participant_public_id)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   participant_private_id participant_public_id
#>   <chr>                  <chr>                
#> 1 9100037                P001                 
#> 2 9100074                P002                 
#> 3 9100111                P003                 
#> 4 9100148                P004                 
#> 5 9100185                P005                 
#> 6 9100222                P006

Gorilla’s private IDs stay, because they mean nothing outside Gorilla. Free-text answers can still hold personal information such as email addresses, so check the questionnaires before you share them.

Save the tables as CSV files

To continue the analysis in other software, or to share the data, write_gorilla() writes the tables to a folder of CSV files:

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "tidy")
files <- write_gorilla(blind_ids(g), out)
basename(files)
#> [1] "participants.csv"        "trials.csv"             
#> [3] "questionnaires.csv"      "questionnaires_long.csv"

The folder has participants.csv, trials.csv, questionnaires.csv with one row per participant and questionnaires_long.csv with one row per answer. Missing values are empty cells and times are in UTC. With by_task = TRUE, each task gets its own trials file, which keeps only the spreadsheet columns of that task. Existing files are only replaced with overwrite = TRUE.
